pulls.title: AssumeUTXO: replace `loadtxoutset` RPC with a startup arg
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Loading a UTXO snapshot through RPC requires coordinating with the active chain, mempool, caches and advertised services while the node is running.

**Fix:** Replace the `loadtxoutset` RPC with `-loadtxoutset=<file>` and finish importing during chainstate initialization, before networking and mempool loading begin.
Require a receiver that has not advanced beyond genesis, already knows the snapshot base header and has no stored blocks beyond genesis or unfinished reindexing.
This removes runtime activation checks, temporary import cache resizing and service demotion while preserving snapshot validation, resumption and background validation.

pulls.title: cmpctblock: Cache serialized cmpctblock msg for relay [part of prefill series]
pulls.body:
This PR extends the optimization added in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/23880 which applies to peers that have requested HB blocks from us to also cache the serialized blocks for low-bandwidth peers. The core change here comes from the closed #26755 made by andrewtoth, but also includes other refactors and type safety improvements.

Performance is less critical for low-bandwidth peers, so this change on its own should have little impact on block propagation, but these refactors are useful as part of https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35558 which adds prefilling of compact blocks, and where we run the risk of potentially having to serialize more than one cmpctblock_msg (one prefilled and one not-prefilled).

pulls.title: txindex: allow running in pruned mode
pulls.body:
After #35531, each txindex entry now points to the block hash containing the tx instead of the file location of the block. The block hash is then used to find the file position of the block to read the tx from. This allows us to determine the hash of the containing block even if the block is later pruned, and also determine the location of the block on disk if it is later downloaded again via `getblockfrompeer`.

This PR enables maintaining a txindex while pruned. If a txid lookup tries to read a tx from a pruned block, the hash of the missing block is surfaced to the caller.

If desired, a user may call `getblockfrompeer` using the returned hash to download the block, then try again successfully. The downloaded block will be added to the front of the block queue, so won't be pruned again for at least 288 blocks. Of course a larger prune setting is desired if lots of historical blocks will be read, and there are privacy issues if the user is looking up their own transactions. Ideally the blocks can be fetched from a trusted node or from random peers with decoy blocks fetched occasionally.

Resolves https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/10609, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/12651, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/16182, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/35240

pulls.title: kernel: make btck_witness_stack_get_item_at O(1)
pulls.body:
Since #36895, `btck_witness_stack_get_item_at` walks the items before the one it returns, so reading a whole witness stack through it is O(n^2).

This keeps a span for each item in `btck_WitnessStack`, which makes `btck_witness_stack_get_item_at` O(1) without changing its signature. `btck_transaction_input_get_witness_stack` is O(n) instead of O(1), because it finds every item when it creates the witness stack.

Breaking changes:
- `btck_transaction_input_get_witness_stack` returns an owned `btck_WitnessStack*`, which must be destroyed with `btck_witness_stack_destroy`.
- The C++ wrapper's `WitnessStackView` is removed, and `GetWitnessStack()` returns a `WitnessStack`.

pulls.title: Add output script index and corresponding script history RPC
pulls.body:
Add a new index `txoscriptindex` which indexes all output scripts. Introduce a new `getscripthistory` RPC that returns all transactions that create outputs corresponding to the provided scripts, and optionally the transactions that spend those outputs if `txospenderindex` is also configured.

This has been a long-requested feature, attempted in previous PRs (#2802, #3652, #6835, #10370, #14053).
Some concerns raised were about the ability for an index like this to scale. I think the new techniques being used to build the indexes (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35531, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36002) alleviate this concern. This index can be synced in a few hours and the current disk usage is ~54 GB. This is less than the ~66 GB `txindex` disk usage in v31 and earlier. This index can also be used with a pruned node, so a full node can be supported in < 100 GB of disk space. Missing blocks are returned by hash and can be requested from peers using `getblockfrompeer`.

Some other previous concerns were more conceptual, that this type of index could encourage address reuse and chain analysis. IMO this ship has sailed, and the current status quo of not shipping an address index is turning off users who expect this functionality. Workarounds involve installing, configuring, and syncing other third-party software, making the UX of using Bitcoin Core in a self-sovereign way unnecessarily difficult.

The index hashes each output script with SHA256, then applies salted SipHash-1-3-UJ and stores a six-byte prefix. This is to support the popular Electrum protocol, which supplies only the script hash. The RPC can also look up by address or descriptors. Ranged descriptors are also supported, so a single RPC call can return the entire history of a receive/change xpub pair.

Keys contain the six-byte script-hash prefix followed by a three-byte big-endian block height. This lets LevelDB seek directly to the prefix + block height, so we can page by block height range.

To prevent DoS concerns by supplying an address with millions of outputs, the RPC tracks a byte budget of reads and throws immediately if too many reads are attempted. The error message instructs the user to narrow the block range.

Improvements to `txospenderindex` (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36480) will also allow us to use that pruned. The end result would allow users to run with all optional indexes (including this one) in < 200 GB of disk space. Of course a larger pruned setting would be desired if many historical block lookups were being requested.

pulls.title: ci: add native freeBSD ci job
pulls.body:
This replaces the FreeBSD cross-compilation job with a native build and test job inside a FreeBSD VM. NetBSD and OpenBSD retain their existing cross-compilation jobs.

We currently cross-compile BSD binaries without testing them in this repository. Running tests before merge should help catch platform-specific regressions that would otherwise first appear in nightly builds. This starts with FreeBSD because it has been the most reliable BSD platform in the nightly jobs.

As we don't have native FreeBSD runners, the job uses [vmactions/freebsd-vm](https://github.com/vmactions/freebsd-vm), which is also used by the nightly builds. It reuses the existing CI scripts, depends build, and cache actions where possible.

The VM image is cached after its `prepare` step installs dependencies. The job also restores and saves the usual build caches. Initial testing on free GitHub Actions runners took approximately 60 minutes without caches and 20–30 minutes with caches populated. Performance on Warp runners remains untested.

The VM uses the runner's available CPU count and 75% of its RAM, leaving the remaining memory for the host and VM overhead. There is some overhead after testing while `rsync` copies cache directories back out of the VM.

The patchset also suppresses `lsof` warnings on FreeBSD that would otherwise interfere with functional tests.

The job requires enabling one additional action:

```text
vmactions/freebsd-vm@v1
```

Passing `verbose=1` as the help suggests returns `Unknown named parameter verbose`. The RPC also bypasses the schema’s numeric type check and reports a custom error for boolean inputs.

pulls.title: fuzz: fix timelock range in miniscript_smart
pulls.body:
`ConsumeNodeSmart` draws `older()/after()` values from `[1, 0x7FFFFFF]`, one F short of the `[1, 0x7FFFFFFF] `range used by the stable target. `after()` never reaches `LOCKTIME_THRESHOLD`, so `miniscript_smart` never builds time-based `after()` nodes and never exercises the height/time timelock mixing checks in `ComputeType`.

Use `std::numeric_limits<int32_t>::max()` for the bound in both targets instead of hand-counted hex literals.

With the fix, replaying the existing qa-assets corpus hits the mixing branches that previously had 0 hits (libFuzzer edges go from 8829 to 8841), and a 5 minute run covers the remaining ones. The corpus stays valid since the byte consumption stays the same.

pulls.title: validation: Prevent duplicate logging and looping in invalid block handling
pulls.body:
`InvalidChainFound()` is called from 3 spots:
1. from `InvalidBlockFound()`
2. from `ActivateBestChain()`, with the highest connectable block of the chain
as an arg (after having called `InvalidBlockFound()` already for the block that failed in `ConnectTip()`)
3. from `InvalidateBlock()` (rpc-only)

Most of the logic in `InvalidChainFound()` is not required for 2) and 3):
In `ActivateBestChain()`, the previous call to `InvalidChainFound()` before via `InvalidBlockFound` did the flag updates, best header calculation and logging, so only `m_best_invalid` could need additional updating.
In `InvalidateBlock()` (which doesn't call `InvalidBlockFound()`), we do most of the accounting manually.

Therefore move of all logic but the `m_best_invalid` update into `InvalidBlockFound()`, avoiding duplicate logging and unnecessary work (the loops over the block index in `SetBlockFailureFlags()` and `RecalculateBestHeader()`
were done twice before).

The second commit renames `InvalidChainFound` to `UpdateBestInvalid` to adjust to its remaining role.

This addresses past discussions about repeated work in `InvalidateBlock()` (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31405#discussion_r2135717500) and `ActivateBestChain()` (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31533#discussion_r2607189790)

pulls.title: fuzz: DisableNextWrite in mempool targets
pulls.body:
`AcceptToMemoryPool` and `ProcessNewPackage` end with `FlushStateToDisk(PERIODIC)`. Whether that flush writes depends on `m_next_write`, which lives in the static chainstate and is re-armed after each write. So the following targets leak the next write time from one input to the next:
- `tx_pool`
- `tx_pool_standard`
- `tx_package_eval`
- `ephemeral_package_eval`
- `validation_load_mempool`

Whether an input hits the write path (leveldb, block index, coins sync) then depends on the inputs that ran before it.
This matters because the fuzzer can then save an input for coverage that the input does not reproduce on its own, and a crash in that path may not reproduce from the single input that triggered it.

Fix it the same way `process_message(s)` and `cmpctblock` already do (#32822): call `DisableNextWrite()` at the start of each input.

Measured with `contrib/devtools/deterministic-fuzz-coverage --mode=combined` on qa-assets, comparing hits of the periodic-write branch (`validation.cpp:2839`, `nNow >= m_next_write`) between two shuffled replays:

| target | before (run A / run B) | after |
|--------|------------------------|-------|
| validation_load_mempool | 4 / 8 | 0 / 0 |
| tx_pool_standard | 9 / 5 | 0 / 0 |
| tx_pool | 4 / 17 | 0 / 0 |
| tx_package_eval | 6 / 7 | 0 / 0 |
| ephemeral_package_eval | 7 / 4 | 0 / 0 |

`validation_load_mempool` now passes the combined check. The other four still show unrelated nondeterminism, which this PR does not address:
- the script execution/signature cache shared across inputs;
- the `CoinsTip` cache state, which changes the number of `CCoinsViewDB` reads.

The input format is unchanged, so the qa-assets corpora stay valid.

pulls.title: wallet: only rebroadcast transactions originating from the wallet
pulls.body:
As explained in #3828, rebroadcast of transactions paying the wallet (but not spending any wallet inputs) is a privacy leak, since anyone can generate these, choose a low fee, and observe who rebroadcasts them. 
While it is somewhat intuitive that submitting transactions has privacy implications - at least until confirmation - this is manageable by various strategies (switching to privacy networks for a while, using private broadcast, making sure it confirms before rebroadcast). However, I find it rather unexpected that just passively running a node with a wallet loaded can lead to a loss of privacy as well.

This PR stops rebroadcasting transactions that don't spend any wallet inputs. For the same reason, they are also no longer re-added to the mempool on startup or after an import: otherwise our node might be the only one still having a transaction the rest of the network has dropped, which can be detected with active probing (e.g. by submitting a child).

This does have the trade-off that receivers (who have an incentive to get paid) will now need to manually resubmit transactions if the transaction doesn't confirm and the sender doesn't rebroadcast, but I think it is worth the privacy benefit.

An alternative approach is https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36380, although these could also be combined (make rebroadcast optional, but never rebroadcast non-originating transactions)

Fixes #3828

pulls.title: Detect transaction problems early during deserialization
pulls.body:
This is split off from #36521 (and not included in #36895), as it's effectively an independent improvement.

This introduces a number of additional checks that are applied during transaction deserialization, which reduce various worst case deserialization time scenarios:
* Reject transactions with more txins or more txouts than can possibly fit in a block (applied always)
* Reject transactions with 0 txins or 0 txouts (applied in P2P code only; there are RPCs like `fundrawtransaction` that explicitly support transactions with 0 inputs)

This is a mild behavior change, as detecting these problems early causes them to be treated as deserialization errors, which in P2P logic cause messages to be ignored instead of peer disconnection.

pulls.title: net: defer compact filter requests that race the filter index
pulls.body:
This PR defers cfilter-related P2P messages if they ask for information from a new block which has been validated, but compact filters are not yet constructed. This PR is a prerequisite for a bigger change of decoupling index construction from block connection to make block announcement faster.




Fixes: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/29655, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/27085
Related discussion: [1](https://bnoc.xyz/t/request-block-filter-peers-being-disconnected-due-to-invalid-block-requests/101/2)

When a new block arrives, block connection has several steps (described very broadly):

1) block connection to the active chain
2) and then comes indices construction (compact block filters index, txdindex) and also wallet updates

If a light peer sends `getheaders` after the first step has passed, but the second has not, the light peer would
then send `getcfheaders` (or another cfilter request) with the stop hash of the new block. Core has no filters yet and thus doesn't answer, and the light peer thinks Core misbehaves and disconnects. 

This race condition is extremely rare right now, because normally headers are received via BIP130 and in that case the light client would not receive a new header until Core is ready to serve the filters (Core does not announce block until the filters are constructed, but can respond with a new header if explicitly asked). So to hit the race condition, the light client has to actively poll the Core node with `getheaders`.

Active polling is not prohibited by BIP157 and in my opinion it should not be (at the very least, light clients need
to sync and have to send `getheaders` with a zero stop hash, which might hit the race). Once Core has sent the block in a `headers` reply, the stop hash "is known to belong to a block accepted by the receiving peer".

This race condition would occur far more frequently (on every new block if light client is fast enough) if new header
announcements were made without waiting for index construction (which we'd love to see in the future). It is discussed here: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/35023. In that case light clients would receive new header announcements from Core without the need to actively poll it.

The approach used (via https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/35023#issuecomment-4332885607) is to stop processing all messages from a peer if there is a request from it which we cannot answer right now, but will be able to shortly. So this PR introduces a way to stop processing requests from a peer, which later can be used to park a peer who sent us a new block (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35354#issuecomment-5363737198).

What it adds:

A `getcfilters`, `getcfheaders` or `getcfcheckpt` request that is racing the filter index is parked instead of being ignored:

  1. `PeerManagerImpl::ShouldDeferCFilterRequest` checks whether a request is racing the index construction: the index is synced, but has not yet caught up with the tip, and does not cover the requested stop hash yet. It never defers during IBD, where the index can lag the tip for a long time.
  2. If so, the request is stored in the peer's `m_pending_request` and we stop processing further messages from that peer. This keeps responses in order; other peers and outgoing messages are not affected.
  3. The parked request is retried whenever we process that peer's messages, at most once every 100ms (`PARKED_CF_RETRY_INTERVAL`) to avoid taking `cs_main` too often.
  4. If the request is still parked after 5s (`MAX_CF_PARK_INTERVAL`), we stop waiting and serve what we can: the peer gets the answer if the filters exist by then, otherwise the request is ignored, as it was before this PR. The peer then continues to be processed normally.

A new `cfilter_race_tests` suite (`src/test/cfilter_race_tests.cpp`) uses a `PreFilterBlocker` `CValidationInterface` registered before the filter index, so its own `BlockConnected` fires first on the scheduler thread and stalls it before the filter index gets to run `CustomAppend`. This reproduces the race window deterministically. The tests drive the real message processing path via `ConnmanTestMsg` and advance the mocked clock where time matters.

Cases covered:

  - `deferred_cfilter_response_reaches_peer` — a racing `getcfilters` is parked, not answered and not dropped, and is answered once the index catches up.
  - `deferred_cfheaders_response_reaches_peer` — the same for `getcfheaders`.
  - `pending_request_pauses_message_processing` — while a request is parked, a later `ping` from the same peer is not processed, and the responses come back in request order.
  - `parked_request_retries_are_throttled` — a parked request is not retried before the retry interval has passed, even if the filter is ready.
  - `parked_request_is_released_after_timeout` — after the park timeout the peer is no longer paused (a later `ping` is answered), and no filter is sent for a filter that does not exist.

I've used Claude Code for this PR.


P.S. Light clients (kyoto, neutrino) also do cross-polling: they ask for filters from a peer that didn't announce the
block, naturally receive no answer, and might disconnect it. Disconnection due to cross-polling occurs more frequently than those due to active polling and this PR does not address it directly, as it IMO is a mistake by light clients, not Core's one. Still, this PR gives such cross-polled filter requests an additional window to resolve if the asked node is in the process of filter construction.
Related neutrino discussion: https://github.com/lightninglabs/neutrino/issues/338.

pulls.title: guix: backport oscrypto PBKDF2 timing fix

This PR adds the fix to `contrib/guix/patches`. It can be dropped once a new oscrypto release includes the fix and a Guix time machine bump includes it.

pulls.title: script: store interpreter stack elements as reference-counted objects
pulls.body:
Modifies the script interpreter to represent stack elements internally using smart pointers, making duplication memory-cheap, and giving us caching keys which are cheap and guaranteed unique by the compiler. First part of a 2-part project to improve script interpreter performance in preparation for PQ signatures. 

No consensus changes - a pure performance improvement refactor.

## Motivation 

We presently have `MAX_SCRIPT_ELEMENT_SIZE = 520`, but in the near future, motivated by the need for PQ signature schemes, we may want to introduce soft fork changes which increase the max stack element size for new output types well into the multi-kilobyte range. This may be perhaps as high as 10kb or more given the current landscape of PQ signature schemes' sizes. 

Ongoing related work:

- https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/blob/main/leaf-version-0xC2.mediawiki#user-content-Relaxing_the_Max_Stack_Element_Size
- https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/pull/76

This poses a new problem to today's implementations if deployed naively. 

Today's Bitcoin script interpreter moves around raw mutable byte vectors to represent stack elements. When those elements are duplicated, the underlying byte vectors are deep-copied. When hash opcodes execute, they always invoke the corresponding hash function and fully ingest the top stack element. Duplication and hashing cost only a single weight unit in tapscript, with no upper limit on how many times they can be executed, aside from implicit limits due to the 10,000 byte script size maximum.

If we were to simply up the stack element size limit from 520b to 10kb, then we exacerbate an existing DoS vector on bitcoin nodes: Push a big (today 520b, maybe someday 10kb) stack element, then duplicate and hash it over and over. Worst case would be a script like this:

```cpp
<big_blob> DUP DUP [DUP3 RMD160 DROP RMD160 DROP RMD160 DROP]...
```  

...with the `[...]` part repeating up to the script size limit. RMD160 is used because it lacks hardware acceleration support and so performs significantly worse than even HASH256 or HASH160, making a more effective CPU attack.

This costs the attacker only \~20000 weight units (10kb for the script, 10kb for the stack element), but forces all validators to evaluate OP_RIPEMD160 about 4284 times, each on the same 10kb input. That's about 672588 RMD160 compressions in software.

I ran a benchmark (not in this PR) using this style of script with 520b and 10kb script elements. 

- 520b: validation takes about **3 milliseconds**
- 10,000b: validation takes about **52 milliseconds**

## This PR

(idea credit: EthanHeilman)

To address this risk, we would want to implement a **hash cache** for all the hashing opcodes. However, to implement such a cache safely in consensus, we need extremely robust cache keys. A collision in the cache key would be a consensus bug because the cache would return the wrong hash for a given input. But we can't cryptographically hash the inputs to compute a cache key... that is the same work we are trying to avoid with the cache. 

Instead we can kill two birds with two PRs. 

1. Replace stack elements with ref-counting pointers, so OP_DUP et al duplicate pointers and not the underlying raw bytes. :arrow_backward:  **THIS PR**
2. Implement a hash cache keyed by the stack element pointers. Each cache entry holds a handle to the key pointer so that the key doesn't get dropped and the pointer reallocated for a new stack element (which would cause a consensus bug). Cache key uniqueness is guaranteed by the compiler.  :arrow_backward: **Future PR**

Stage 1 reduces the asymmetric memory inflation attack allowed by OP_DUP et al. Stage 2 fixes the asymmetric CPU DoS attack. To be clear, neither stage fully prevents an attacker from uploading a series of large stack elements, and duplicating/hashing them. But we **do** force attackers to pay for those operations with fees and block space. 

I have both stage 1 and 2 implemented locally and can show benchmarks to prove the effect of the cache, if desired. I could have submitted it all as one PR but both stages are atomic and could do well with separate review.

pulls.title: [wip,nomerge,rfc] build: Require C++23 compiler
pulls.body:
C++23 for Bitcoin Core is mostly a "style update" on top of C++20. However, the workarounds to avoid C++23 keep accumulating and some parts of the code already use C++23 features, such as lambda attributes (https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/commit/bdd0cd69418d189f62699d274a751cbf6d36bb43).

I don't know when it is fine to switch, but at some point, I think it is fine to require a C++23 compiler, so that [new stuff](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/34979#issuecomment-4448399166) is unlocked. Of course this requires bumping the minimum required compiler versions:

* GCC: 13
* Clang: 19

There are some C++23 features that aren't implemented (such as `<stacktrace>` not really shipped in any vanilla stdlib today), or e.g. `ranges::starts_with` not implemented until libstdc++-16. But overall I think we are better off using C++23 without those few features instead of waiting longer?

pulls.title: net: reduce ASMap lookup and address grouping costs
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Addrman groups peer addresses by network prefix or (when ASMap finds a match) by autonomous system.
Without ASMap, grouping classifies the address twice.
With ASMap, an IP lookup allocates a temporary key and the decoder calculates a shift distance for each mantissa bit.
Building the group can also take several allocations for just a few bytes.

**Fix:** When ASMap is disabled, skip the extra address classification in `GetMappedAS`.
Build ASMap lookup keys on the stack and decode integers by shifting each bit into the mantissa.
Reserve space for the address group before appending its bytes.

**Time to group one IPv4 address:** (Raspberry Pi 5, ns per call, lower is better)

```text
                                 With ASMap                    Without ASMap
master      baseline             ███████████████████▉ 1,982    █████▏ 518
80a39cd417  Decode integers      ██████████████████▎  1,830    █████▎ 524
adc7012941  Skip empty map       ██████████████████▎  1,824    ███▉   390
bbe7b52765  Build lookup key     █████████████████▌   1,744    ████   394
13e0803197  Reserve group space  ████████████████▍    1,640    ███▏   307
```

Across the full series, `AddrManAdd` is 19.2% faster (59.1 to 49.6 ms).

pulls.title: [Demo] validation: remove AssumeUTXO
pulls.body:
**Draft demo:** this is meant to showcase what complete AssumeUTXO removal could look like and the simplifications that AssumeUTXO currently prevents.
The decision about complete removal is of course still open. This draft is meant to serve as a concrete reference for the smaller proposals below - it's not meant to be merged.

**Smaller PRs:** I will carve out individual changes to gauge interest in each part, and link them here as they are opened.
Some of the findings are useful even if snapshot loading or background validation stays.
Feedback on which parts seem worth pursuing, and in which order, is welcome.

**Motivation:** this follows our in-person discussion at the October 2026 Core Dev meeting.
My impression was that there was rough agreement about the ambiguity background validation introduces: we trust a snapshot enough to use it immediately, but describe that trust as temporary until the same node finishes checking history.

Multiple chainstates affect much more than snapshot loading: ordinary validation changes have to account for different chainstate roles, candidate sets, notifications, downloads, pruning, cache allocation, database lifetimes and locks.
I am not sure this amount of complexity in the most critical part of our codebase is still worth it, given that adoption [isn't where we hoped it would be](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35054#issuecomment-4468360424).
Ordinary IBD is also getting faster: #35295 is already merged, and the upcoming `pruneassumevalid` will make pruned IBD even faster.

Snapshot bootstrapping without background validation can still offer an advantage: a new node becomes usable before ordinary IBD would finish because snapshot loading time scales with the UTXO set size, while ordinary IBD time scales with the blockchain size.
Whether that is worth its maintenance cost is a fair question, and we can discuss it here or in the dedicated PR where I will propose the removal.
Even after removal, we could decide to add it back in a cleaner way, for example isolated through IPC.
This demo makes that cost, and the code we could remove, visible for that discussion.

**Background validation can be considered separately:** if we keep snapshot loading, I would prefer making its trust assumption explicit and distributing verification across ordinary IBD nodes, as proposed in #32377 and #36543.
That could give us wider independent checking of the commitment without making every snapshot user maintain a second chainstate.

Users who want to validate history themselves and transition to an archival node could rebuild with `-reindex` and pruning disabled.
Alternatively, they could run IBD in a separate datadir while their snapshot node remains usable, then switch once it is ready.
@Sjors's #36557 discusses dropping mandatory background sync and these alternatives.

**What the series demonstrates:**

* After the fixture cleanup in #36601, the next eight commits remove background validation while snapshot loading keeps working, a stopping point that can be reviewed on its own.
* The middle commits remove snapshot imports and startup resumption, then the validation, block storage, notification and release-process special cases they needed.
* The final seven commits add the simplifications this removal enables: startup in one pass, stable database ownership, one download path, a single prune height, and removal of the locks and diagnostics used to select and identify chainstates.

Ordinary validation, `-assumevalid`, pruning, `ChainstateManager` and UTXO export (`dumptxoutset`) remain.

**Related work:**

* [AJ's recent faster-loader branch](https://github.com/ajtowns/bitcoin/tree/202610-loadtxoutset-speedy) and [Sjors's chunked-import experiments](https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/tree/2026/10/utxo-coin-chunks) explore reducing import overhead while retaining snapshot support.
* #35054 contains the broader discussion about P2P snapshot distribution, its users and its costs.

pulls.title: coins,dbwrapper: make point-read and txindex lookup failures fatal
pulls.body:
**Problem:** #34931 made unreadable coin entries fatal, but `CDBWrapper::Read()` still returns `false` for deserialization failures and propagates LevelDB point-read exceptions to callers.
A corrupt txindex point read can consequently fail one RPC while the node continues running.
#35728 reports other txindex lookup failures as errors that callers can also catch while the node continues running.
Chainstate also retains `CCoinsViewErrorCatcher` as a separate view layer to report read errors and abort.

**Fix:** Make LevelDB point-read and typed deserialization failures fatal in `CDBWrapper`, after logging the database path and error and notifying the database owner’s `kernel::Notifications` when supplied.
This includes point-read failures during startup, which now bypass the GUI’s database rebuild offer.
Missing keys still return `false`, database-open failures retain their initialization handling, and iterator behavior remains unchanged.

Pass each owner’s existing notifications at construction for chainstate, the block-index database, optional index databases, and the temporary UTXO database used by `dumptxoutset`.
Remove `TryRead()` and `CCoinsViewErrorCatcher`, keep `HaveCoin()` on the cache view that owns its caching behavior, and mark coin-view lookups `noexcept`.

Make txindex consistency errors and block-file lookup failures fatal through the shared notification path before aborting.
Continue skipping stale entries for unknown blocks and non-active blocks without data.
Direct block reads retain their existing RPC error handling.

pulls.title: rpc: fix a race between `scantxoutset` calls
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Overlapping `scantxoutset` calls can leave the node reporting "Scan already in progress" until restart, even though the scan has finished. A new caller can acquire the reservation while progress from the previous scan is still nonzero. The progress check then throws before the caller records that it owns the reservation, so its destructor never releases it.

**Fix:** Reset progress while the finishing scan still holds the reservation.

**Historical context:** [Luke pointed out](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/19362#discussion_r463934011) that a failed progress check could block all future scans.

pulls.title: rpc: Report -rpcwhitelist denials as JSON-RPC errors
pulls.body:
This PR adds two JSON-RPC error codes for requests refused by `-rpcwhitelist`, which until now got an HTTP 403 status with an empty body:

- `RPC_METHOD_NOT_PERMITTED` (-38) is returned for a refused request, with HTTP 200 for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests and 403 for legacy 1.x requests.
- `RPC_REQUEST_NOT_EXECUTED` (-39) is returned for the other requests in a refused batch. A refused batch now gets HTTP 200 and an array with an error for each request, and still runs none of them.

**Problem:** `-rpcwhitelist` errors are currently handled differently from other JSON-RPC errors, so clients report them with vague or misleading messages, and for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests the handling does not follow [documented behavior](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/doc/JSON-RPC-interface.md#json-rpc-11-vs-20). Specifically, requests refused by `-rpcwhitelist` get HTTP 403 with an empty body, so the refusal shows up as a generic transport error rather than a specific JSON-RPC error. This is especially a problem for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests, which are [supposed to](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/bf1a1f1662427fbf1a43bb951364eface469bdb7) report failed method calls only as JSON-RPC errors, not HTTP errors. The empty reply causes a concrete problem when JSON-RPC requests are sent over IPC instead of HTTP: `bitcoin-cli -ipcconnect` receives only the response body, so a refused call prints a JSON type error instead of a permission error, as described in a [private security review](https://ipcbugs.ofsky.org/audits/ar-56/). Over HTTP, `bitcoin-cli` currently stops at the 403 status and prints only "server returned HTTP error 403" instead of the actual error.

**Solution:** Report whitelist denials like any other failed call: a JSON-RPC error in the body, with the HTTP status the request's version calls for. This brings the behavior in line with the documentation. `bitcoin-cli` then prints the permission error over both HTTP and IPC, with no change to the IPC interface. The fix is a small change to `src/httprpc.cpp` and `src/rpc/protocol.h`, with tests in `rpc_whitelist.py` and `interface_ipc_cli.py`. It comes after two refactoring commits suggested in #36642, which move connection fields out of `JSONRPCRequest` into a new `JSONRPCClient` struct and move the batch loop into a `ProcessBatch()` helper that the refused-batch reply shares. Details in the commit messages.

Compatibility: HTTP clients that send `"jsonrpc": "2.0"` or batches and check for a 403 status need to read the error code instead. Single 1.x requests keep the 403 status, now with an error body.

Open question for review: `RPC_METHOD_NOT_PERMITTED` could be named `RPC_ACCESS_DENIED`, and `RPC_REQUEST_NOT_EXECUTED` is documented as batch-specific but would fit any request refused before it runs.

pulls.title: net, http: handle socket errors separately from reads
pulls.body:
On Linux a socket error or hangup is reported whether or not we asked for it. If that happens for a peer we did not request to read from, disconnect directly. This just adds clarity: previously we would attempt a send that would then fail. The only side-effect is a changed log message. Nothing changes on other platforms: since bitcoin/bitcoin#36716 they no longer report errors for established connections.

The last commit does the same for HTTP, where on error it also no longer attempts a final read from a client whose reads are paused.

As a followup to bitcoin/bitcoin#36716, `p2p_socket_errors.py` adds coverage for existing behavior:
- the node ignores a single urgent byte: the connection stays open, ordinary data is still processed and the urgent byte is not counted as received.
- a peer resets the connection while the node's send to it is stalled and receiving from it is paused: the node disconnects without reading anything more (the change above only changes the log message)

Similarly `interface_http.py` checks that:
- a single urgent byte does not disturb an ordinary request.
- a client reset while the server has unsent responses (the HTTP change only changes the log message)

The first commit drops a comment from the `wait_ignores_urgent_data` unit test, as suggested in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36716#discussion_r4700726004.

To support the new tests, the test framework gains:
- `wait_for_send_stall()`, moved out of `p2p_ping_ibd.py`
- a `reset` option for `peer_disconnect()`, which closes the connection with a TCP reset
- `mine_large_block()` returns the block hash and size
- `pack_linger()`, and `linux_host` / `windows_target` to tell which log message to expect

pulls.title: refactor: Use CBlockIndex parameters as reference
pulls.body:
This is a janitorial refactor, a continuation of #34440. Input method parameters of type `const CBlockIndex*` are changed to reference `const CBlockIndex&` in some places where it makes no sense to call with a nullptr.

Motivation: slight improvement in code quality, maintainability and robustness.
- more explicit representation of the non-null input invariant
- less chance of nullptr-access error with future code changes
- more explicit checks at call sites for the non-null input invariant.

The following methods are affected:
- `LastCommonAncestor()` in chain.h
- `PeerManagerImpl::FindNextBlocks()` (net_processing.cpp)
- `PeerManagerImpl::TryDownloadingHistoricalBlocks()` (net_processing.cpp)
- `BlockFilterIndex::LookupFilterRange()`, `BlockFilterIndex::LookupFilterHashRange()` (blockfilterindex.h), and `LookupRange()` in blockfilterindex.cpp
- `BaseIndex::ProcessBlock()` (base.h)

General guidelines:
- When a method has an input of type `const CBlockIndex*`, and by contract it cannot be nullptr, change it to `const CBlockIndex&`. The reference type is an implicit documentation of the nun-nullptr invariant.
- When calling a method with reference parameter, ensure that it cannot be nullptr (it is often derived from a pointer), by/because:
  - explicit prior check and error handling
  - an assert/Assert/Assume
  - itself being a non-nullptr invariant input
  - it is being an output from a method with no-nullptr output invariant
- For local variables, use reference types whenever possible, for non-nullptr references
- For technical reasons pointers are still used even in some non-nullptr cases:
  - containers/variables that can staty unitialized initially
  - containers that need `reserve()`
  - using reference type in `std::set` would result in some copy constructor calls
  - `std::optional` cannot hold a reference type

pulls.title: txorphanage: bound orphan memory by storing transactions serialized
pulls.body:
The orphanage limits the "usage" of the orphans it stores, per peer and globally, to bound the amount of memory an attacker can make us hold on to. It uses weight as a proxy for that memory, on the assumption that weight is "often higher than the actual memory usage of the transaction".

That assumption does not hold for a deserialized transaction. Every witness stack element is an individually heap-allocated vector, costing its 24-byte slot in the stack vector plus a 32-byte minimum allocation, while only weighing 2WU. A transaction of 199,000 1-byte witness elements weighs 398,247WU (i.e. it is of standard weight, and witness standardness cannot be checked while the inputs are missing), but uses 11.1MB of memory: 28 times what is accounted for it, and one such orphan can be retained per peer.

Rather than change the accounting metric, keep orphans in serialized form, deserializing them again on the paths that hand them back out. Serialized, a transaction's memory usage is bounded by its weight, so the existing weight-based accounting becomes a true upper bound on memory and the worst case is the peers' combined allowances.

Admission, eviction and accounting behavior are unchanged: no transaction that was previously accepted is refused, so orphan resolution (and thus 1p1c package relay) keeps working for standard-weight transactions whose witnesses consist of many small elements, such as BitVM-style transactions.

pulls.title: http: disconnect clients that never finish a request
pulls.body:
The -rpcservertimeout timer only measures inactivity. Every read from a client resets it, so a client that keeps sending bytes without ever completing a request can hold the connection for ever. 

Connection slots are capped by default 16 or by -rpcmaxconnections. Once those slots are taken, the server stops accepting new connections. Because no request ever completes the authentication functions are never hit. 
The impact is low because RPC port binds to localhost by default, so this is a robustness fix rather than a remotely exploitable security issue.

<details> <summary> How to reproduce </summary>

To reproduce: start a node with -rpcmaxconnections=2, open two sockets, and write "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n" one byte at a time with ten seconds between bytes. bitcoin-cli getblockcount then hangs until one of the (trickling) sockets is closed.

</details>

The fix adds a second deadline next to the idle timer. It is armed on the first byte of a request and expires after -rpcservertimeout (the same value as the idle timer). This timer also does not resets or is extended by later reads. Completing request parsing clears the deadline, so a long-running RPC keeps its connection as before. The deadline is deferred while a worker holds the request, for the same reason the idle timer is. It is restarted while response bytes
are written, because the client cannot start a new request during that window. -rpcservertimeout=0 disables both timers. No new option is added.

Disclaimer this bug is found by utilizing ASTRA. Verified using KIMI 3 and Claude.

pulls.title: test: cover missing BIP352 cases
pulls.body:
The existing BIP352 tests leave several cases insufficiently covered. To identify these gaps, I ran manual mutation testing against `src/common/bip352.cpp`. Out of 49 mutations, 27 survived with the existing tests.

With these tests, 47 of the 49 mutations are detected. The two remaining mutations are equivalent to the original implementation.

One mutation replaces the `return std::nullopt` with `break` when `GetOp` fails while scanning a P2PKH scriptSig. The function reaches the same `return std::nullopt` after the loop. The other removes the early return for the case where there are no eligible keys, checking only whether there are no inputs. With no keys, libsecp256k1 already returns a failure, so the result remains `NOT_ELIGIBLE`.

The new tests cover scan label reporting, P2PKH public key extraction when the `scriptSig` contains unrelated pushes, invalid public keys across supported input types, P2SH-P2WPKH eligibility, Taproot script-path spends, annex handling, control block validation, prevouts summary errors, and Silent Payments destination validation.

The existing `bip352_skips_transactions_spending_unknown_segwit_versions` test is also extended to cover SegWit versions v2 through v16 and check the exact `NOT_ELIGIBLE` error. The address decoding tests also cover a v0 address with a valid Bech32m checksum but one extra data byte (67 instead of 66).

The changes are limited to `src/test/bip352_tests.cpp`. No production code is modified.

The tests also pass on top of the P2SH changes from #36776. The annex-related mutations are detected independently of #36992.

`src/common/bip352.cpp` is not included in the continuous mutation-testing runs on corecheck, so these gaps are not covered by those runs.

pulls.title: mempool: recalculate stale BIP68 lockpoints in removeForReorg
pulls.body:
When a reorg lowers the tip, `removeForReorg` can evict BIP68 transactions that are still valid at the new tip, together with all their descendants.

A transaction that spends an unconfirmed parent gets its lockpoints cached with that input at height tip+1. After `invalidateblock`, `TestLockPointValidity` can still pass on those cached lockpoints (always when every input was unconfirmed, since `maxInputBlock` is then genesis; and with mixed confirmed and unconfirmed inputs when the confirmed input's block survives), so `CheckSequenceLocksAtTip` is evaluated against stale values and the transaction is removed.

The fix, suggested by ismaelsadeeq, is to never evict on cached lockpoints alone: if they are not valid at the new tip, or the cached sequence-lock check fails, recalculate them with `CalculateLockPointsAtTip` and evict only if the fresh result also fails. This covers height-based and time-based locks alike, at the cost of some recalculations that turn out to be unnecessary.

test_reorg_stale_lockpoints() in feature_bip68_sequence.py covers four cases across a reorg: a BIP68-disabled child, a BIP68-enabled child of an unconfirmed parent, a child with mixed confirmed and unconfirmed inputs, and a time-based zero lock where the reorg lowers the median time past (test by Bicaru20). The test fails on master, and the mixed-input case also fails on the earlier genesis-only version of this fix.

test_reorg_unsatisfied_lock_evicted() (by instagibbs) is the counterpart: it checks that transactions whose relative lock is genuinely unsatisfied after the reorg are still evicted, together with their descendants.

Reproducer for unpatched nodes:
https://gist.github.com/javierpmateos/c55d365973adbf488a852dc5e0b77dec

Same class of issue fixed for TRUC in #33504.

Closes #35007

pulls.title: p2p: replace full outbound peers that don't support tx relay (take 2)
pulls.body:
Picks up #28538

Outbound-full-relay slots should be used by peers that actually relay transactions, besides #28538 see #16418 and #28371 for the motivation. So try to replace peers that are not relaying txs with peers that do.

The approach differs from the original PR in a few details in response to some of the review comments there:

- A replacement is connected before the peer is evicted. The original PR disconnected a non-tx-relaying peer once all full outbound slots were filled. Reviewers preferred having a replacement available first (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#issuecomment-1883481846). Now an extra outbound-full-relay connection is requested, like the extra network-specific peers, and the existing eviction of extra outbound peers prefers peers that don't relay txs.
- Peers not relaying txs don't get `m_protect`. Otherwise they could stay forever (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#discussion_r1443336121), and ignoring the protection was rejected in the same thread (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#discussion_r1443312604).
- An only peer on a network is not replaced. Otherwise the network-specific extra connections and this logic would keep replacing each other (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#issuecomment-1883481846). This also covers the `-maxconnections=1` case (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#discussion_r1417178196).

Nothing is changed in `-blocksonly` mode or during IBD. The rename commit and the functional test are taken from the original PR with some changes to match the new behavior.

pulls.title: test: avoid BSD ephemeral-port collisions in HTTP clients
pulls.body:
While stress-testing #36147 I noticed sporadic port collisions still occurring on FreeBSD.

`set_ephemeral_port_range()` keeps the source port out of the test port range, but only for sockets the framework creates itself. Python's `http.client` creates its sockets internally, so RPC and REST connections can still be given a source port inside the test range. A connection to a closed port can then connect to itself. For example, the wrong-RPC-port startup check failed with `BadStatusLine: POST / HTTP/1.1` because the client read back its own request.

This change adds a `netutil.HTTPConnection` subclass that sets the port range before connecting, and uses it in `AuthServiceProxy` and in the tests that open HTTP connections directly.

HTTPS is left unchanged because we don't serve RPC over TLS so it seems unnecessary.

pulls.title: RFC: netbase: Remove manual_connection and return the failure reason to callers
pulls.body:
Based on #36969, only the last commit is new. Draft to see if this direction is wanted. This also came out of discussions in #36759: 

The `manual_connection` flag of `ConnectDirectly()` only picks the log level of a failed `connect()`. Callers that are not manual peers, like Tor control, pass `true` just to get the failure logged, and the caller that knows how much a failure matters never sees the reason.

This removes the flag. `ConnectDirectly()` returns the failure reason and each caller decides how to log it. The log output stays the same, except that manual peers and Tor control now log every failure reason at info level, including timeouts, which were debug only.

pulls.title: net: serve `MSG_BLOCK` by stripping witnesses in place
pulls.body:
**Problem:** To send a `MSG_BLOCK` reply from disk, a node currently decodes the block and serializes it again without witnesses.
For `MSG_WITNESS_BLOCK`, it already sends the stored bytes directly.
Serving `MSG_BLOCK` efficiently also matters for the proposed witnessless initial block download. [#36476](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36476)

**Fix:** For `MSG_BLOCK` replies from disk on non-Signet chains, read the block into an owned byte buffer and check the header’s proof of work and expected hash.
Walk the serialized transactions directly and strip their witnesses in place.
Signet still uses `ReadBlock` to verify the Signet solution.
Header checks now run before transaction parsing, so if both the header and transaction data are corrupt, the node may log a different error.

**Performance:**
| Block | Before | After | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `block413567` | 3.204 ms | 0.369 ms | **8.7×** |
| Same block with synthetic witnesses | 8.944 ms | 1.026 ms | **8.7×** |

The synthetic fixture adds a 512-byte witness item and an empty item to every input.

**Related work:** This extends the path that sends witness blocks directly from disk. [#13151](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13151)
Earlier work identified unnecessary transaction hashing when serving historical blocks. [#13011 discussion](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13011#issuecomment-383145046) · [#13098](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13098)
The implementation also builds on bulk block reads. [#31551](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31551)

pulls.title: bip352: match P2SH-P2WPKH instead of evaluating it
pulls.body:
For P2SH inputs, `GetPubKeyFromInput` evaluated the full scriptSig with `EvalScript` and then ran `Solver` on the redeem script, even though only P2SH-P2WPKH is eligible for BIP-352. That costs time on every non-segwit P2SH spend (e.g. multisig), whose scriptSigs can be up to `MAX_SCRIPT_SIZE`.

BIP-141 requires the scriptSig of a P2SH-wrapped witness program to be exactly a single push of the redeem script (`SCRIPT_ERR_WITNESS_MALLEATED_P2SH`). So any valid P2SH-P2WPKH scriptSig is exactly `0x16 OP_0 0x14 <20-byte keyhash>`, and matching that template gives the same result without evaluating anything.

### Benchmarks

`bench_bitcoin -filter='BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_.*' -min-time=2000`, Release build.

Before:

|            ns/input |             input/s |    err% |     total | benchmark
|--------------------:|--------------------:|--------:|----------:|:----------
|              688.30 |        1,452,858.07 |    0.1% |      2.20 | `BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_Multisig`
|            7,158.19 |          139,700.11 |    0.1% |      2.20 | `BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_P2WPKH`

After:

|            ns/input |             input/s |    err% |     total | benchmark
|--------------------:|--------------------:|--------:|----------:|:----------
|               56.87 |       17,584,611.40 |    0.0% |      2.20 | `BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_Multisig`
|            6,949.45 |          143,896.18 |    0.0% |      2.20 | `BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_P2WPKH`

P2SH multisig is about 12x faster to rule out. P2SH-P2WPKH saves about 200 ns per input; its time is still dominated by `CPubKey::IsFullyValid()`.

pulls.title: mining: use a steady clock for the getblocktemplate rebuild interval
pulls.body:
Based on #36356 and #36921. **Only the last commit is new.**

After a mempool change, `getblocktemplate` only rebuilds its cached template once it's more than 5 seconds old, and it measures that age with the system clock. That works fine in practice, but as pointed out in a [review comment](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36356#discussion_r4562199844), a steady clock is the better fit for measuring an interval, since system time changes don't affect it.

This switches to the steady clock, like #30372 did for `RandAddSeedPerfmon`. Since `setmocktime` doesn't move it, `mining_prioritisetransaction.py` now waits out the 5 seconds, and the unit test uses a fake steady clock.

pulls.title: blockstorage: fix partial-mask assertions and genesis availability checks
pulls.body:
**Problem:** `CheckBlockDataAvailability` checks whether the upper block has any requested bit. `GetFirstBlock` requires every requested bit, so a partial match can reach its assertion. At genesis, the existing undo exception can reject an undo-only request or accept a request with missing block data. It also misses ranges containing only genesis.

**Fix:** Require every requested bit on each block in the range, except that genesis needs no undo data. An empty mask now succeeds for a valid range because it requests no bits. Both index-startup calls supply nonempty masks.

pulls.title: test: fix `mining_prioritisetransaction` check that always passes
pulls.body:
`mining_prioritisetransaction.py` checks that `prioritisetransaction` alone makes `getblocktemplate` return a new block, by comparing the whole template before and after moving mocktime 10 seconds forward. But `curtime` comes from the clock, so the two templates always differ, even if the template wasn't rebuilt.

This PR checks that the deprioritised transaction drops out of the template instead. 
If you remove the counter bump in `CTxMemPool::PrioritiseTransaction` (the fix this check was added for in #10196), the test from master still passes but this one fails.

pulls.title: init: Fix surprising behaviors of negated options
pulls.body:
While looking into #36759 I discovered `-notorcontrol` did the opposite of what would be expected from it and I then checked for similar issues in other init options. There are several more where `-nofoo` does something surprising including one of them crashing the node.

This PR attempts to fix all these surprising behaviors while also keeping things as simple as possible and just change behavior to something that makes sense harmless in the context of the option. Fixes that use a common approach for the fix are grouped together into a commit even if the options included themselves may have no relation at all.

| Commit | Problematic options behavior | Fix approach |
|---|---|---|
| [mempool: Reject cluster limits below 1](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/512773d111daaa4330c873ed5889b9ef511f6e3a) | `-nolimitclustercount` hits an assertion in `TxGraph` on the first mempool transaction. `-nolimitclustersize` rejects every transaction. | Reject values below 1 at startup. |
| [args: Add NEGATE_TO_EMPTY so -nofoo reads as an empty string](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/ac4b8feb3fe151d1b00085cfe15a856ccede6e6e) | `GetArg()` returns `"0"` for a negated option. The `-no*notify` options run the command `0`, `-nosigner` uses `0` as signer, `-noi2psam` fails startup and `-norpcpassword` sets the password to `0`. Opt-in because options like `-noonion` and `-noblockfilterindex` depend on reading `"0"`. | New opt-in flag `NEGATE_TO_EMPTY` makes `GetArg()` return `""`. |
| [init: Read -cjdnsreachable and -help as booleans](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/dc4ddbacf791ac6742261bf66dcf42887bfb74ff) | `-cjdnsreachable=0` and `-nocjdnsreachable` turn CJDNS on. `-nohelp` prints the help. | Use `GetBoolArg()` instead of `IsArgSet()`. |
| [args, wallet: Fix empty and negated -blocksdir and -walletdir](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/be71581c2fc65722f6e335e6506cda342eb23ef7) | `-noblocksdir` writes block files relative to the working directory. `-nowalletdir` fails startup. | Fail at startup with `DISALLOW_NEGATION`. An empty value falls back to the default directory, like `-datadir` does. |
| [init: Require -nolistenonion with -notorcontrol](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/44b1c5b05057bf3a768eac63922c085163975dcc) | `-notorcontrol` connects to `0.0.0.0:9051`, which reaches a local Tor. | Fail at startup unless `-listenonion` is disabled. |
| [init: Disallow negating options where it has no meaning](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/6447b07919072f12aba36313814fd4962dd4363a) | `-nocheckblocks`, `-nomaxreceivebuffer`, `-nomaxsendbuffer` and `-nomaxtipage` read as 0, the opposite of what the user asked for. | Fail at startup with `DISALLOW_NEGATION`. |

`-nomempoolexpiry` has a similar kind of problem. It evicts transactions as soon as the next one arrives. I left it out because #36540 already is open and addresses this.

pulls.title: rpc: generateblock to allow multiple outputs with custom payouts
pulls.body:
## Generatetomany

First approach was to create a `generatetomany` rpc call. That approach can be seen here https://github.com/polespinasa/bitcoin/pull/3

## Generateblock
Modifies `generateblock` to allow a user to set multiple outputs in the coinbase transaction. If an empty set is provided, the block will be empty. If no set of transactions is provided, the block will mine the mempool. If a set of transactions is provided only that set of txs will be mined.

```
$./bitcoin-cli -rpcport=18443 generateblock bcrt1qw6qkj8wtw5hraxwxjp08m4aymkntms3yhqyacj
{
  "hash": "7359a3ed7af0f18f4016e6cb29193bd787a2452c584781135c585d5204b9ec5b"
}

$ ./bitcoin-cli -rpcport=18443 generateblock '["bcrt1qal6p633hvwz2yp5mav0qy7u2az8gkn2xywnj6v", "bcrt1qvr3qgyhw6y0e0zj97v0j5yc40xtpea4wqj0g43"]'
{
  "hash": "6db028454b26d6667dd6df45be2772844121fb44f86433f6bbfbafa429974684"
}

$ ./bitcoin-cli -rpcport=18443 generateblock '["bcrt1qal6p633hvwz2yp5mav0qy7u2az8gkn2xywnj6v", "bcrt1qvr3qgyhw6y0e0zj97v0j5yc40xtpea4wqj0g43"]' []

{
  "hash": "33e2ddc52546ddb0edf28bef5b295ee8fbd487b8aca19c97018467e2477877df"
}

```

### Motivation
https://x.com/SuperTestnet/status/1921220086645342550

Citating @supertestnet 
> When mining a block on regtest, the command "generatetoaddress" is available if you want to send the entire coinbase to 1 address. Let's add generatetomany in case you want to split up the coinbase among multiple addresses, similar to how the "sendtoaddress" and "sendmany" commands both exist and let you send money to (1) one address or (2) multiple addresses. The generatetomany command would be particularly useful for simulating protocols that send money to multiple recipients directly from a coinbase, as several pools do now, like ocean and braidpool.

pulls.title: validation: Ensure Invalid ValidationState has result
pulls.body:
Block and transaction validation results are represented in `ValidationState`, and invalid results in "Invalid" states. Invalid validation results have a `result`, an enum value, and a `reject_reason`, a structured string.

The change is to ensure that an __invalid result always has a set result and reject reason__. This increases code robustness/security.

One instance was identified where the result was not set, and is being fixed by a new `BLOCK_INCONCLUSIVE` result. PR #31981 moved a previous-block check from outside of `TestBlockValidity()` to inside it, and introduced a new usage of `BlockValidationState` with unset result. The result field is not checked outside. This instance is changed now to use the newly-introduced `BLOCK_INCONCLUSIVE` value.

The new enum value is added to the kernel C API and its C++ wrapper. In P2P, a `BLOCK_INCONCLUSIVE` result does not lead to punishing the peer.

A few test-only instances with empty reject reason are changed to use a dummy value ("dummy-reason").

History: this was found on the side of #35570, but left untouched there; see https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35570#issuecomment-5739477357 and https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35570#discussion_r4075379069.

Alternatives considered:

1. Use a new reject reason enum. This is the cleanest solution, but the cost is the extension of a widely-used validation enum.
2. Use a different mechanism for returning this specific case from `TestBlockValidity()`, e.g. using `util::Expected`, as you discussed. No need to touch the `BlockValidationResult` enum. However, in the call sites of `TestBlockValidity()`, the reject reason and debug strings are handled similarly to other non-valid check results, and they would need a special handling.
3. Reuse an exisiting reject reason enum value in `TestBlockValidity()`, with the comment "only in this spot it means a little different thing".
4. Create a special `TestBlockValidationResult`, "on top of" `BlockValidationResult`, with the extra value, and a special `TestBlockValidationState` (`ValidationState<TestBlockValidationResult>`). Use this in `TestBlockValidity()`. As this is used only internally, within this methods and at its call sites, the new value+state doesn't have to be exposed. Therefore the change has lower impact.

replaces the magic number 6 in the trailer boundary condition with kHeaderSize and corrects an off-by-one by expressing the rule as offset_in_block > kBlockSize - kHeaderSize, which is equivalent to offset_in_block >= kBlockSize - 6. According to 
src/leveldb/doc/log_format.md:
“A record never starts within the last six bytes of a block” 
and when exactly seven bytes remain a record may start (e.g., a zero-length FIRST), so the equal case must be treated as trailer. The writer already uses kHeaderSize to manage trailers, and aligning the reader with kHeaderSize removes a format-coupled magic number and ensures future-proof consistency. Functionally this avoids scanning a block when initial_offset_ is in the last six bytes, matching the documented format; it was previously a minor inefficiency and comment mismatch rather than a correctness issue.

pulls.title: wallet, rpc: Add analyzedescriptor for multisig setups
pulls.body:
Part of the multisig setup work tracked in #35645. Based on #35918 (the first 3 commits).

Before importing a multisig descriptor received from a coordinator, each participant needs to check that it is the setup they agreed on: a k-of-n where any k cosigners can spend and nothing else can, that their own key is in it, and that they all derived the same first address. Today nothing in Core reports what a descriptor commits to, so tools had to parse the descriptor string by hand, as the multisig wizard in #36325 (now closed) did.

This PR adds that check in three layers:

1. **Inspection** (commits by w0xlt, with small changes listed below): `GetKeyInfo()`, `GetKeyInventory()` and `GetPolicy()` describe a parsed descriptor's key expressions, where each key is used, and how they combine. `getdescriptorinfo` gains a `verbose` option that returns them as `keys` and `policy`.
2. **Multisig analysis, no wallet:** `AnalyzeDescriptor()` tells whether a descriptor is a recognized k-of-n setup, and if not, why. `getdescriptorinfo verbose` returns it as `analysis`, so it works even with `-disablewallet`.
3. **Wallet part:** `interfaces::Wallet::analyzeDescriptor` (for the GUI) and the `analyzedescriptor` wallet RPC add which keys the wallet holds, whether it can sign, and the first receive address. They accept any descriptor, single-sig included; `analysis.recognized` tells whether it is a safe k-of-n.

Recognized setups are `wsh(multi)`/`wsh(sortedmulti)`, and `tr(K,multi_a)`/`tr(K,sortedmulti_a)` with a single leaf, where `K` is the BIP 341 NUMS point or a `musig()` of at least k distinct cosigners. Every cosigner must be an extended key with an unhardened ranged derivation, and no two cosigners may be the same key. Anything else is still analyzed and returned, with `recognized: false` and the list of issues: the analysis warns, it never refuses a descriptor.

Example, run by one of the three cosigners:

```
$ bitcoin-cli -rpcwallet=alice analyzedescriptor "wsh(sortedmulti(2,[a1b2c3d4/48h/1h/0h/2h]tpub.../<0;1>/*,...))"
{
  "keys": [
    { "role": "ecdsa", "type": "bip32", "xpub": "tpub...", "derivation": "/0/*",
      "origin": { "master_fingerprint": "a1b2c3d4", "path": "m/48h/1h/0h/2h" }, "wallet": "mine" },
    { ..., "wallet": "not_mine" },
    { ..., "wallet": "not_mine" }
  ],
  "analysis": { "recognized": true, "shape": "wsh_multi", "sorted": true, "threshold": 2, "cosigners": [0, 1, 2], "issues": [] },
  "can_sign": true,
  "first_address": "bcrt1q..."
}
```

A **locked wallet** is not an error: a cosigner key with a hardened origin path can't be checked without the private key, so it is reported as `"unknown"`, and `can_sign` is left out unless another key is already known to be the wallet's. Everything else (`analysis`, `first_address`) is still returned, and the caller can ask the user to unlock and retry. Only the candidate private key is decrypted.

#### Commits

| | Commit | Author |
|---|---|---|
| 1‑3 | #35918 | pseudoramdom |
| 4‑7 | key/policy inspection, `getdescriptorinfo verbose` | w0xlt (see changes below) |
| 8 | `script: add AnalyzeDescriptor() for multisig setups` | co-authored with w0xlt |
| 9 | `rpc: add multisig analysis to getdescriptorinfo verbose` | |
| 10 | `wallet: add analyzeDescriptor to the wallet interface` | co-authored with w0xlt |
| 11 | `rpc: move descriptor key and analysis JSON helpers to a shared file` | move-only |
| 12 | `wallet, rpc: add analyzedescriptor` | co-authored with w0xlt |


#### Changes made to the inspection commits (4-7)

The inspection commits come from w0xlt's descriptor inspection [branch](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/compare/master...w0xlt:bitcoin:feature/descriptor-key-inspection-simplified). These changes were made on top, for w0xlt to review and agree with or not (this section will be removed once agreed):

- *script: expose key expression structure* (was "expose structured key program data")
  - Use `m_root_extkey` instead of `*GetRootExtPubKey()`.
  - The derivation test also covers `/0h/*` and `/1/*h`, checking the last-hardened and derived caches.
  - `wide += ')'` instead of `")"` in the participant test (clang-tidy `performance-prefer-single-char-overloads`).
- *script: identify descriptor key occurrences*
  - `KeyRole()` is pure virtual; descriptors without key arguments (`addr`, `raw`, `sh`, `wsh`) say so explicitly with `NONFATAL_UNREACHABLE()`.
  - Comment noting that `frame` is invalidated by the following `push_back`.
  - The walletload test mock is reduced to `return {}`.
- *script: expose descriptor policy nodes*
  - The header documents the two forms of the same construct (descriptor function vs Miniscript fragment).
  - `Assert` → `CHECK_NONFATAL`; explicit `static_cast<uint32_t>` for the threshold.
  - The fuzz target checks where each child role may appear (tap leaves only under `tr`, `script` only under `sh`/`wsh`, the Taproot internal key only on `tr`, the output key only on `rawtr`).
- *rpc: add verbose option to getdescriptorinfo*
  - The multipath note moved to the `verbose` argument help; the `policy` help explains both forms.
  - Tests for an origin without a path and for MuSig participant origins.

Open question: `script/descriptor_analysis.h` describes and gives no verdict, while `script/descriptor_analyzer.h` gives the verdict; the names are easy to mix up. Rename the first to `script/descriptor_inspection.h`?

#### Design choices

- An unrecognized descriptor claims no setup: no threshold, cosigners, sorting or key path. For example `wsh(sortedmulti(2,A,A,C))` is not a 2-of-3, since A alone can spend. Each issue lists the key IDs involved instead.
- The same xpub with different paths in two cosigner slots is a `repeated_key`, as is an xpub and its own child xpub. BIP 388 allows the same key with disjoint paths in general policies, but in a k-of-n it lets one holder fill two slots.
- A Taproot key path is either `nums` or `musig`. Any other internal key, a `musig()` of fewer than k cosigners, or one with an outsider or a repeated cosigner is `key_path_spendable`.
- For a multipath descriptor every path is analyzed and must be the same setup (`branches_differ` otherwise). `keys` and `policy` describe the first path.
- `can_sign` means the wallet holds the private key for at least one key of the descriptor, whatever its shape. Whether it is a safe k-of-n is a separate answer, `analysis.recognized`.

The functional test scenarios of #36325 were adapted here. The analysis differs from that wizard in a few places:

- `wsh(multi(...))` is recognized, with `sorted: false`: it is a valid k-of-n, and requiring `sortedmulti` was the wizard's own policy.
- A `musig()` key path of at least k distinct cosigners is recognized: those cosigners can already spend through the leaf.
- A single-path descriptor (`/0/*`) is recognized; `multipath_expansion` already shows whether it is multipath.

#### Known limits

- A cosigner key is matched against the wallet's HD keys exactly, or by deriving its origin path from the HD key with that fingerprint (normally the master key). If the wallet only holds an imported account xprv, keys below it are matched only exactly.

A release note will follow.

pulls.title: [RFC] ipc: add Events interface for chain and mempool notifications
pulls.body:
This adds an Events IPC interface that streams block and mempool events in one ordered stream, addressing gaps in ZMQ notifications and providing a more modular interface. It supports the following subscriptions:

- `blockConnected`: fires for every block connected to the active chain, including during IBD (blocks connected by a background assumeutxo chainstate are skipped). Carries hash, height and optionally the serialized block. ZMQ `hashblock`/`rawblock` are driven by UpdatedBlockTip, so they skip intermediate blocks when several connect at once and don't fire during IBD.
- `blockDisconnected`: fires for every block disconnected during a reorg, with hash, height and optionally the serialized block.
- `txAddedToMempool`: fires only for mempool acceptance. Carries txid, wtxid, mempool sequence, fee, vsize and optionally the serialized tx. ZMQ `hashtx`/`rawtx` also fire for every tx in connected and disconnected blocks, so a subscriber can't tell whether a tx entered the mempool (pain point of https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/19462#issuecomment-658304417, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/23624#issue-1065790580 and https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/7753).
- `txRemovedFromMempool`: fires for every removal, including txs removed because they were mined (reason `block`), except during IBD, with txid, wtxid, mempool sequence, removal reason and optionally the serialized tx.

ZMQ `sequence` covers all four of these, but only carries hashes (plus the mempool sequence for "A"/"R"), and "R" doesn't include block-inclusion removals or a reason.

Why not just do it with ZMQ?

- One ordered stream that includes the data. `rawblock`/`rawtx` have their own sequence numbers and can't be ordered against `sequence`. Here every event can include its serialized block or tx in the same ordered stream. Events come in the same order as ZMQ `sequence`, plus block-inclusion removals.
- Typed, versioned interface. Cap'n Proto generates the client code and lets the schema [evolve without breaking older clients](https://capnproto.org/language.html#evolving-your-protocol). With ZMQ, clients parse raw bytes by hand which can't evolve existing topics without breaking changes.
- Fixing these in ZMQ would need new topics reporting on the same events as existing ones, which is confusing for users, and changing the existing topics would break current consumers.
- Bounded buffering. Events are buffered per subscription up to a byte limit (`-ipceventsbuffer`), and the client pulls them in batches with waitNext. ZMQ limits are message counts per topic (-zmqpub*hwm), which don't bound memory when messages are full blocks.

Why additional data, including derivable ones?

- fee, vsize: neither can be derived from the tx alone, so including them saves RPC calls per tx. RPC calls can also fail if the tx was removed in the time in between.
- mempool sequence: lets a client line events up with `getrawmempool` (`mempool_sequence=true`) to bootstrap and keep a mempool mirror in sync.
- height: not in the serialized block, and needed to handle reorgs without an extra RPC call.
- hash, txid, wtxid: identifiers are always included, so clients don't need to branch on `include_data`.

Example of simple clients using this interface, including a mempool mirror: https://github.com/ViniciusCestarii/bitcoin-ipc-events-client

Note: to make this interface usable in this PR, the Cap'n Proto `union` that this uses is mapped by hand in `events-types.h`. Ideally this support would be added to libmultiprocess first.

pulls.title: rpc, wallet: Convert walletprocesspsbt to use options parameter
pulls.body:
This picks up #24963.

`walletprocesspsbt` takes four settings after the PSBT, three of them booleans, so a positional call reads `walletprocesspsbt "psbt" true "ALL" true false`, and each new setting becomes one more positional parameter (#32857 would add a sixth). - `getopenrpcinfo` describes the second parameter as an object or a boolean.
- A call mixing positional and named arguments, such as `walletprocesspsbt <psbt> true finalize=false` with `-named`, works as on master instead of failing with "specified twice".
- The type check by name no longer reads the wrong name after an options object built from named options, which made `walletcreatefundedpsbt outputs=... add_inputs=true bip32derivs=false` fail with "JSON value of type object is not of expected type object".
